# King's Scholar – Exclusive Summary
The title "King's Scholar" originates from a writ issued by King Edward II in 1317, establishing the first group of King's Scholars at Cambridge, composed of twelve boys from his household whose expenses were paid for by the crown. In 1440, King Henry VI founded Eton College as a charity school for "poor, scholarly boys." By 1443, Eton formally recognized 70 King's Scholars housed in the central College building, distinguishing them from fee-paying students (“Oppidans”).
At Eton College today, King's Scholars (also called "Collegers" or "tugs") are selected via a competitive exam and awarded a Foundation Scholarship, gaining entry into the house called "College." At any time there are about 70 King's Scholars, aged 13–18, identified by wearing black academic gowns. They share most activities with Oppidans but have exclusive traditions, such as eating in College Hall and extended participation in the Wall Game. Historically, Foundation Scholarships covered all fees, but now scholarships are means-tested and may not cover fees unless financial need is demonstrated. Scholars have the post-nominal "KS" in school lists. Academically distinguished Oppidans may become Oppidan Scholars ("OS") but do not receive financial benefits.
Beyond Eton, "King's Scholar" refers to scholars at Westminster School, King's College Cambridge (for undergraduates with first-class degrees), and to recipients of King's Scholarships at seven King's Schools re-founded by Henry VIII in 1541, including King's Ely, King's School Canterbury, and King's School Worcester. Scholars at these institutions are granted various privileges—such as ceremonial rights, the option to marry or be buried in cathedral grounds, and the wearing of distinctive gowns—and may, in some schools, be joined by Queen's Scholars when the reigning monarch is female.
Many notable public figures are former Eton King's Scholars, including writers (George Orwell, Aldous Huxley), scientists (J.B.S. Haldane, Henry Moseley), Prime Ministers (Robert Walpole, Harold Macmillan, Boris Johnson), and diverse leaders in law, academia, and the arts.
